blocks.text: Once vectors exist, the next natural question is what happens when you combine them. Addition and subtraction are the two simplest, most common ways to combine vectors, and they turn out to be exactly the operations behind averaging embeddings, updating weights during training, and even the famous king minus man plus woman example that first made word embeddings go viral.

blocks.alt: Two vectors branching into addition producing a sum vector and subtraction producing a difference vector
blocks.caption: The two operations this lesson covers, side by side.

blocks.text: 1. Adding Two Vectors
Adding two vectors is done component by component: add the first numbers together, add the second numbers together, and so on. There is nothing more to it arithmetically than that.

code.content:
a = [3, 2]
b = [1, 3]
result = [a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1]]
print(result)   # [4, 5]

import numpy as np
print(np.array(a) + np.array(b))   # [4 5]

blocks.text: This works for vectors of any length, not just two numbers, provided both vectors being added have exactly the same number of components. Adding a 4-number vector to a 3-number vector is simply not defined, there is no third number to pair the extra one with.
1.2 Adding Vectors of More Than Two Dimensions

Nothing about the rule changes once a vector grows past 2 or 3 components. A 768-dimensional embedding gets added to another 768-dimensional embedding the exact same position-by-position way, just repeated 768 times instead of twice.

code.content:
a = np.random.rand(768)
b = np.random.rand(768)
result = a + b
print(result.shape)   # (768,), same shape as the inputs

blocks.text: 1.1 The Tip-to-Tail Picture

Geometrically, addition means drawing the first vector, then drawing the second vector starting exactly where the first one ended, tip to tail. The sum is the single arrow that goes directly from the very start to the very end of that two-step path.

blocks.alt: Vector a drawn first, then vector b starting from the tip of a, with the sum a plus b drawn directly from the start to the final tip
blocks.caption: Walking a, then walking b, ends at the exact same spot as walking a plus b directly.

blocks.text: 2. The Parallelogram Picture

There is a second, equally valid way to picture the same addition: draw both vectors starting from the origin, then complete the parallelogram they form. The diagonal of that parallelogram, starting at the origin, is the sum.

blocks.alt: Vectors a and b drawn from the origin, completing a parallelogram whose diagonal is a plus b
blocks.caption: Both pictures, tip-to-tail and the parallelogram, always agree, they are just two different ways of drawing the identical result.

blocks.text: This parallelogram view also explains why vector addition never depends on which vector is drawn first, walking along the bottom-then-right edge of the parallelogram or the left-then-top edge both land on the exact same opposite corner.
2.1 Why Two Pictures for One Operation

It can feel strange that the same addition has two different-looking diagrams. They are not actually different, the parallelogram is just the tip-to-tail picture drawn twice, once for a followed by b and once for b followed by a, both paths sharing the same start and the same end point, which is exactly why a plus b equals b plus a.
3. Subtracting Two Vectors

Subtraction works the same way, component by component, just with subtraction instead of addition. This is exactly the gap vector introduced in the vector representation lesson: a minus b points from b to a.

code.content:
a = np.array([4, 3])
b = np.array([1, 5])
print(a - b)   # [3 -2]
print(b - a)   # [-3 2]

blocks.text: It is worth noticing that subtraction can be rewritten as addition of a negative: a minus b is exactly the same as a plus the negative of b, where negating a vector simply flips the sign of every component. Some libraries and mathematical proofs prefer working with this addition-only framing since it avoids treating subtraction as a separate operation with its own rules.
3.1 Order Matters for Subtraction

Unlike addition, subtraction cares deeply about order. a minus b and b minus a are the exact same length but point in exactly opposite directions, a fact worth keeping straight since it is easy to mix up under pressure.

blocks.title: A quick way to remember it
blocks.content: a minus b points from b to a, arriving at a. Read it right to left: start at b, arrive at a.

blocks.text: 4. Why Addition and Subtraction Matter in AI

items: Averaging embeddings: adding several word vectors together and dividing by how many there are, a simple way to build one embedding for a whole sentence.
Gradient descent updates: a model weight vector is updated by subtracting a small multiple of the gradient vector from it at every training step.
Measuring change: subtracting an old embedding from a new one shows exactly how, and how much, something shifted.

blocks.text: 4.1 A Famous Example: King Minus Man Plus Woman

One of the most famous demonstrations in embedding research showed that taking the vector for "king", subtracting the vector for "man", and adding the vector for "woman", lands remarkably close to the vector for "queen". The model was never told this relationship directly, it fell out of the arithmetic because the direction from "man" to "king" and the direction from "woman" to "queen" turned out to be nearly the same vector.

blocks.alt: Four points, man, king, woman, and queen, with the same vertical arrow representing "becoming royal" going from man to king and from woman to queen
blocks.caption: The same arithmetic step, adding the same royalty vector, connects man to king and woman to queen.

code.content:
king = model["king"]
man = model["man"]
woman = model["woman"]
result = king - man + woman
# result ends up extremely close to model["queen"]

blocks.text: This result is not perfect in practice, the actual closest vector to the computed result is usually queen, but not always exactly, and the margin depends heavily on how the specific embedding model was trained. Even so, the fact that simple vector arithmetic captures a real conceptual relationship at all was a genuinely surprising and influential discovery.

This example is worth revisiting once cosine similarity is covered later in this module, since checking whether the computed result is actually close to queen means measuring similarity, not exact equality, between the computed vector and every candidate word vector in the model vocabulary.
5. Commutativity and Associativity

Addition is commutative, a + b always equals b + a, and associative, grouping does not matter, (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c). Subtraction is neither: a minus b does not equal b minus a, and changing the grouping in a chain of subtractions changes the answer.
5.2 Why This Matters for Averaging Order

Because addition is commutative and associative, summing a list of embeddings in any order, or in any grouping, for example across parallel batches that get combined afterward, always produces the exact same total. This is a genuinely useful guarantee for distributed systems that split an averaging computation across multiple machines and combine partial sums later.
5.1 Checking Associativity With Real Numbers
Seeing this proven with actual numbers makes it more convincing than the abstract rule alone.

code.content:
a = np.array([1, 1])
b = np.array([2, 0])
c = np.array([0, 3])
print((a + b) + c)   # [3 4]
print(a + (b + c))   # [3 4]

blocks.text: 6. Adding More Than Two Vectors: Averaging

Addition extends cleanly to more than two vectors at once, simply add all of them component by component. Dividing that sum by how many vectors were added gives the average, one of the most common ways to combine multiple embeddings into a single representative vector.

Averaging is a simple technique, and it is worth being aware of its limits too. It treats every input vector as equally important, which is not always true, a sentence embedding built by averaging word vectors, for example, cannot tell that word order matters, since shuffling the words averages to the exact same result.

Averaging is really just addition followed by one extra scalar division step, tying this section directly back to the scalar broadcasting covered in the very first lesson of this module, dividing every component of a summed vector by the same single count.
6.1 Seeing the Averaging Pipeline

blocks.alt: A flow diagram showing several word vectors being summed and then divided by their count to produce one average sentence vector
blocks.caption: The same addition covered earlier in this lesson, just run across many vectors instead of two.

blocks.text: 7. A Worked Example
Take the two vectors used throughout this module, A at (4, 3) and B at (1, 5), and compute both their sum and their difference.

code.content:
a = np.array([4, 3])
b = np.array([1, 5])
print(a + b)   # [5 8]
print(a - b)   # [3 -2]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operation","Result","Plain description"],"rows":[["A + B","(5, 8)","Further right and further up than either vector alone"],["A minus B","(3, -2)","Points from B to A"]]}

blocks.text: 8. Subtraction and Distance, Connected Directly

The magnitude lesson computed distance as the length of the vector connecting two points, without dwelling on how that connecting vector is actually produced. It is produced by exactly the subtraction covered in this lesson: distance between A and B is nothing more than the magnitude of A minus B.

code.content:
a = np.array([4, 3])
b = np.array([1, 5])
distance = np.linalg.norm(a - b)
print(distance)   # about 3.606

blocks.text: This single line connects three separate lessons in this module into one sentence: subtract two vectors, then measure the magnitude of the result, and you have the distance between them.
Distance itself is really just this lesson and the magnitude lesson working together: subtract two vectors to get the gap between them, then measure how long that gap is.

It is worth remembering this connection specifically because it means every distance calculation anywhere in this platform, no matter how it is described in words, is doing nothing more than these two operations, subtraction and magnitude, back to back.
9. A Small Application: Nudging an Embedding
Adding a small vector to an existing embedding is how a model gently adjusts a representation without discarding it entirely, whether that nudge comes from a training update or a deliberate edit.

blocks.alt: A large blue vector representing an original embedding, with a small red vector added at its tip representing a small nudge
blocks.caption: A small addition shifts the result slightly without changing its overall character much.

blocks.text: The size of the nudge relative to the original embedding matters a great deal here. A tiny addition barely changes the direction at all, while a large one can swing the result toward a completely different meaning, which is exactly the balance a learning rate is trying to strike during training.

The direction of the nudge matters just as much as its size. A nudge added in a consistent, meaningful direction across many examples, rather than a random one, is exactly how a model learns to shift its internal representations toward better predictions over the course of training.
10. Practice: Add and Subtract These
Try computing (2, 5) + (3, -1) and (2, 5) minus (3, -1) by hand before checking below.

blocks.title: Answers
blocks.content: Adding gives (2 plus 3, 5 plus negative 1), which is (5, 4). Subtracting gives (2 minus 3, 5 minus negative 1), which is (-1, 6). Notice subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its positive, which is why the second component grew instead of shrinking.

blocks.text: If either answer felt uncertain, it is worth writing out each component separately on paper, add the first components together, then separately add the second components, rather than trying to do the whole vector operation in one mental step.
11. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming subtraction is commutative like addition, a minus b and b minus a point in opposite directions.
Trying to add or subtract two vectors of different lengths, the operation is only defined when both vectors have the same number of components.
Forgetting to divide by the count when averaging several vectors, which leaves a sum rather than an average.
Expecting an analogy like king minus man plus woman to land exactly on the target word, in practice it lands very close, not perfectly on top of it.

blocks.text: Reviewing this list before writing any code that adds, subtracts, or averages vectors is a fast habit that catches the majority of bugs this specific area of AI code tends to produce.

Between this lesson, magnitude, and the upcoming dot product lesson, nearly every distance and similarity calculation used anywhere else in this platform can be traced back to some combination of these few, simple building blocks.
Key Takeaway

Vector addition combines two vectors component by component, and can be pictured either tip to tail or as the diagonal of a parallelogram, both describing the exact same result. Subtraction works the same way arithmetically but is order-sensitive, a minus b points from b to a, the opposite direction of b minus a.

These two simple operations are doing real work throughout AI systems: averaging turns many embeddings into one, gradient descent subtracts its way toward a better set of weights, and the famous king minus man plus woman example shows that meaningful relationships between concepts can literally be captured as consistent vector arithmetic.
